scenes.tts: One generation after heavy-labelled E coli switched to ordinary nitrogen, all of its DNA formed one band. That band sat halfway between heavy and light. Why did none remain fully heavy?

scenes.visual: Open directly on a 16:9 caesium-chloride tube filling most of the frame. A PURPLE heavy band at the bottom dissolves, and one GOLD band settles halfway between labels 'heavy' and 'light'. Above it, a large purple duplex slowly turns. The question 'Why halfway?' appears. Colour map for both films: parental DNA PURPLE, new DNA CYAN, observations GOLD, eliminated models RED, enzyme blocks GREEN, RNA primers YELLOW. Keep a small 'schematic' label at bottom right. The band shimmers and the duplex drifts throughout.
Over the carried tube and drifting duplex, fade in the title 'What the Halfway Band Means' for two seconds. Keep the GOLD band gently shimmering.

scenes.tts: To follow old DNA, Meselson and Stahl grew cells with heavy nitrogen. Old strands appear purple; strands built after the switch appear cyan. In a caesium chloride gradient, heavy DNA settles lower than light DNA. Hybrid DNA settles between them.

scenes.visual: The purple duplex stretches into two labelled PURPLE strands. A CYAN strand slides beside one purple strand to make a hybrid duplex. At right, the same large tube gains three labelled landing guides: 'heavy' low, 'hybrid' middle, 'light' high. A purple duplex, purple-cyan duplex and cyan duplex drift to those positions in turn while the liquid continues a slow swirl.

scenes.tts: Three models start from the same purple duplex. Conservative copying keeps both old strands together and builds a separate cyan duplex. Semiconservative copying separates the old strands, then gives each a new partner. Uniform dispersive copying breaks the old material into segments and mixes those segments through both daughters.

scenes.visual: Move the starting duplex to centre. It transforms three times in the same location under a changing model label. 'Conservative': one intact purple duplex and one cyan duplex pull apart. 'Semiconservative': purple strands unzip and each receives a cyan partner. 'Uniform dispersive': each strand transforms into alternating purple and cyan rectangular segments. Never show molecular bonds. Keep at most the two daughter cartoons and one label visible.

scenes.tts: A band is not a picture of a helix. It marks many DNA molecules with the same buoyant density. One intermediate band could mean every molecule is half old. It cannot reveal whether that half is one intact strand or many segments until another generation separates their predictions.

It cannot reveal whether that half is one intact strand or many segments until another generation separates their predictions.

scenes.visual: Zoom into the GOLD hybrid band until it becomes a crowd of many small duplex cartoons. Half are purple-cyan hybrids; they transform into evenly segmented purple-cyan duplexes without moving the band. A large bracket labels the crowd 'same buoyant density'. The two internal patterns alternate slowly while the band position remains fixed.

scenes.tts: Watch each model make its initial daughters. Which models can put every molecule at the hybrid position, with no heavy or light band?
scenes.narration: Watch each model make its initial daughters. Which models can put every molecule at the hybrid position, with no heavy or light band?
scenes.caption: Watch each model make its initial daughters. Which models can put every molecule at the hybrid position, with no heavy or light band?
scenes.visual: Arrange three large tubes across the frame, labelled 'conservative', 'semiconservative' and 'uniform dispersive'. Above each, its daughter cartoons hover. Band guides are empty. The question 'Which can make only a hybrid band?' spans the top. Daughter cartoons bob gently toward their tubes but do not settle yet.
Deliberate thinking pause. Hold the three empty tubes and the question. The daughter cartoons continue a slow hover; liquid in each tube swirls gently. Do not reveal any band.

scenes.tts: Conservative copying makes one heavy duplex and one light duplex. A single hybrid band after one generation rules out conservative copying. Semiconservative copying makes two purple-cyan hybrids. Uniform dispersive copying can also put equal old and new material in every molecule. Both survive the initial test.

scenes.visual: The conservative daughters settle into separate low PURPLE and high CYAN bands; a RED outline closes around that tube and the model label dims. In the other tubes, purple-cyan hybrids and segmented duplexes settle into GOLD middle bands. A small GOLD observation marker aligns with both surviving bands. No word such as 'extinct' appears.

scenes.tts: Now let the survivors copy again in ordinary nitrogen. Semiconservative copying keeps each purple strand in one hybrid. The other daughters are fully cyan. Its tube gains separate hybrid and light bands. Uniform dispersive copying halves the old fraction inside every molecule again. Its single band shifts toward light.

scenes.visual: Remove the dimmed conservative tube. In the semiconservative lane, each carried duplex opens and receives cyan partners; purple-cyan hybrids settle at the middle guide while cyan duplexes settle high. In the dispersive lane, purple segments shrink as cyan segments expand, and every duplex settles together above the former middle position. Bands and molecules move together throughout.

scenes.tts: After two generations, the extracted DNA formed hybrid and light bands in equal amounts. That matches the semiconservative distribution, not one uniformly mixed band. Hybrid and light bands after two generations rule out uniform dispersive copying. The old material never disappears. It only spreads among more molecules, and where it sits is decisive.

scenes.visual: A GOLD observation tube slides over the semiconservative tube; its equal middle and high bands align exactly. The dispersive tube remains beside it with one shifted band, then receives a RED outline and dims. The number of purple label particles in both lanes stays constant while cyan material grows around them; only the semiconservative lane sorts them into separate molecule types.

scenes.tts: The experiment tracked inherited material, not enzymes. Heating the hybrid DNA separated heavy and light subunits, consistent with old and new strands. Meselson and Stahl still stated their limit carefully. Their bands did not alone show that each conserved subunit was one polynucleotide chain.

scenes.visual: Return to one large purple-cyan hybrid duplex over the tube. A heat-wave icon passes across it; the two coloured subunits separate and settle at heavy and light guides. A bracket labelled 'consistent with strands' appears, followed by a smaller question tag 'subunit identity?'. Do not show an enzyme or atom-level structure.

scenes.tts: Each daughter molecule keeps one old strand and builds one new strand. That logic predicts later band patterns and gives replication its name: semiconservative. Keep the rule for chromosome replication in this lesson.

scenes.visual: A single purple parental strand grows large across the frame. One cyan partner builds beside it from left to right as small rectangular blocks join. The pair settles above the GOLD hybrid band. The label 'semiconservative' appears beneath, while unused tubes and model labels fade away.

End card with one line only, in large centred white text: 'Each daughter molecule keeps one old strand and builds one new strand.' Behind it, one purple and one cyan strand drift together slowly. No title, subtitle, logo line or smaller text appears.
